title: LIVE: Anders Hejlsberg on TypeScript’s Go Port
summary: Matt Pocock interviews Anders Hejlsberg, Technical Fellow at Microsoft and lead architect of TypeScript, days after the announcement that TypeScript is being ported to Go. Anders describes the 10x speedups the team is already seeing (compiling VS Code drops from about 70 seconds to 7) and the roadmap to command-line-compiler parity within months, with JSX and JSDoc support being rearchitected along the way. He explains the compiler's four phases - parse, bind, check, emit - why parse, bind, and emit are embarrassingly parallel, and how checking is parallelized by splitting the program's files across four independent checkers that share only an immutable program view, deliberately duplicating some type-resolution work to avoid any synchronization, with deterministic error ordering as the hard constraint. The conversation covers the WASM tradeoff (Go must emulate stack switching, so the browser target currently gives the gains back and runs about as fast as the old compiler), why Go beat Rust (no new memory-management scheme and no breaking cyclic data structures), pool-allocating AST nodes to cut allocations by two orders of magnitude, and why only a port - not a rewrite - can reproduce the old compiler's semantics in excruciating detail. He finishes on backwards compatibility as a religion, the ~100,000-test baseline suite that gates every merge, regrets like namespaces and parameter properties, erasable syntax, and type checkers becoming fast semantic oracles that AI agents can query through protocols like MCP.
what_you_learn: You get systems-design lessons straight from a 40-year language architect: how to parallelize work deterministically over immutable shared state, why porting beats rewriting when correctness is the product, what allocation-level performance engineering looks like with a real profiler, and how a checked-in baseline snapshot suite enforces compatibility across a rewrite. For agent work specifically, Anders sketches the emerging pattern of exposing a language service as a semantic oracle that AI tools query via MCP - fast, verifiable ground truth for the code a model just generated.

skills.name: Software Architecture
skills.description: Type syntax that tools can strip, making transpile-free TypeScript viable through bundlers and Node's type stripping.

skills.name: AI Output Verification
skills.description: Parallel checking that produces identical output on every machine, regardless of core count.

skills.name: Testing Strategy
skills.description: Checked-in snapshots of every test's symbols, types, and error messages; any diff must be analyzed before merge.

learnings.title: The 10x speedup and the road to parity
learnings.detail: Anders confirms the numbers behind the announcement: VS Code compiles in about 7 seconds instead of 70, with zero errors, and deliberately introducing an error still gets caught - compiling clean is not an existence proof. The first parity milestone is the command-line compiler, expected within a few months; JSX and JSDoc are being rearchitected rather than ported because the team now knows better ways to build them. Projects using only .d.ts files with no TSX or JSDoc are already close to usable.

learnings.title: The public API problem: from 'the code is the API' to an exe behind LSP
learnings.detail: A major unknown unknown. In JavaScript the compiler's API was effectively its entire implementation, and the ecosystem partied on every internal detail. The Go compiler is a binary with nothing to call unless the team designs it: LSP (the language server protocol) is definitely in, as a veneer around the compiler - the semantic oracle that answers what is the type of this and what are its members - but a performant, versionable API that reveals the right details is still being explored, and IPC costs now matter where in-process calls did not.

learnings.title: WASM gives the gains back - for now
learnings.detail: Answering Evan You's concern about Go-on-WASM: the team built a WASM target and found it runs about the same speed as the old compiler - acceptable, but the 10x is gone. The root cause is Go's need for lightweight stack switching (green threads): WASM abstracts the stack so goroutines must emulate it, which is costly, and WASM GC cannot be used until it integrates with stack switching, so Go drags its own garbage collector into the box. Anders expects this to improve over time and considers the tradeoff acceptable, noting Rust might target WASM better but would have brought worse problems.

learnings.title: Why Go and not Rust
learnings.description: The port needed a native language but could not afford a new memory-management scheme: TypeScript's compiler data structures are cyclic (symbols point to types point back to declarations), and Rust has no good answer for cycles without contorting the design. Go's everything-is-functions-and-data-structures model, garbage collection, and goroutines fit the existing architecture; the full rationale lives in Ryan Cavanaugh's GitHub discussion, which Matt links in the description.

learnings.title: Four phases, and three are embarrassingly parallel
learnings.detail: Anders breaks compilation into parse (source to AST), bind (find declarations, build simple scope tables), check (walk each AST, resolve names and types, verify compatibility), and emit (TypeScript to possibly down-leveled JavaScript). Parse and bind create one goroutine per source file and scale linearly, modulo IO bandwidth when every goroutine wants to read a file at once. Check is different: it needs the whole-program view because resolving one identifier can jump across imported modules.

learnings.title: Concurrent checking: split files across independent checkers over an immutable program
learnings.detail: The classical approach - one threat-safe checker with mutexes on shared mutable structures - would be a huge undertaking full of contention. Instead, the parse and bind output is immutable by design (built once per file even when a file belongs to multiple projects), so checking splits the program's files into chunks and spawns four checkers, each given the full program view but responsible for only its quarter of the files. They duplicate some shared-type work but need zero synchronization, run at full throttle, and finish with a harvest step that dedupes the error lists.

learnings.title: Deterministic output beats using every core
learnings.detail: Ordering matters: elaborated explanations should appear once, not flood the output, and which checker resolves a type first depends on scheduling. If the checker count adapted dynamically to CPU count, a CI machine with fewer cores would produce different errors and break baseline comparisons. So the axiom is: results must be deterministic across builds, and today that means hardwiring four checkers - leaving maybe 20 percent on the table (eight checkers would be faster and hungrier), which is not worth the risk for a 7-second vs 6-second difference.

learnings.title: Native code kills JIT sponginess and enables allocation engineering
learnings.detail: JavaScript JITs made performance profiles spongy: change code over here and the JIT deopts something over there, leaving background-radiation noise you cannot profile away. Native Go is predictable, and pprof quickly revealed the allocation strategy as the hotspot. The big trick: 30-40 percent of AST nodes are identifiers, all the same size, so instead of allocating one at a time (which keeps the GC visiting millions of tiny objects), a per-parser pool allocator grabs chunks of 256 and hands them out sequentially - cutting allocation counts by two orders of magnitude. Removing the pool allocators would halve the compiler's speed.

learnings.title: Backwards compatibility is king - and it dictates port, not rewrite
learnings.detail: TypeScript never ships breaking changes: producing more error messages - which is what doing the job better means - can break a build that was clean, so betterness ships under opt-in flags. This philosophy directly explains the port decision: only by porting can you get the same semantics in excruciating detail; a first-principles rewrite would silently diverge. Compilers simply do not have the semver flexibility frameworks enjoy - Go itself is effectively still 1.x for the same reason.

learnings.title: Erasable syntax makes types-as-comments mostly moot
learnings.detail: On the TC39 types-as-comments proposal: simple erasure schemes demand delimiters no one wants, so ergonomics suffer. Meanwhile almost every browser workflow already runs a bundler, and bundlers already erase types - so there is no extra step to avoid. That leaves Node running naked .ts files, which Node now supports via erasable-syntax type stripping. Isolated modules, isolated declarations, and the erasable-syntax-only flag are TypeScript's side of the contract, warning you about constructs that will not survive stripping. Anders sees the need as largely satisfied without changing JavaScript.

learnings.title: Do not spend the 10x on 10x more complex types
learnings.detail: Asked whether the performance budget buys fancier language features: sometimes - the team knowingly paid about 7 percent for a canonical ordering of types that concurrent checking requires. But the real risk is users: the type system is Turing complete, and fancy libraries can simply absorb the 10x by computing types 10x more complex until checking takes 10 seconds again and it feels good enough. Anders's plea: embrace the performance, write responsible types. Proof of Turing completeness: someone ran Doom in the type checker, at roughly one frame per day.

learnings.title: Regrets: namespaces, parameter properties, and the erasable-enums future
learnings.detail: Features Anders would not add today: old-style namespaces (necessary before ES modules existed - the team predates even ES5), parameter properties, and probably classic enums. He still finds enums handy and notes TC39 is warming to them; if Ron Buckton's enums proposal lands, TypeScript will embrace it, possibly in an erasable form (a plain object literal with an as-enum-style modifier). If TC39 ultimately says never, an erasable enums variant is the fallback - but the team wants a JavaScript-sanctioned form first.

learnings.title: The AI opportunity: language services as semantic oracles over MCP
learnings.detail: Beyond faster pipelines, Anders sees the biggest downstream impact in AI integration: protocols like MCP let tools surface a language service to a model, so the model can validate the code it just chunked out, or ask where a symbol is declared - questions only a semantically aware service can answer. Some refactorings may drift toward copilot-like AI features (dreaming up better names) while the base LSP functionality stays deterministic. A year ago the models were not good enough for this to matter; now a 10x-faster checker makes such workflows feasible.

learnings.title: Baseline testing: ~100,000 tests and checked-in output snapshots
learnings.detail: No PR merges unless the full suite - close to 100,000 tests - passes. Beyond pass/fail, every test's output (symbols, types, error messages) is captured as a checked-in baseline artifact; a new compiler version regenerates the artifacts and diffs them, and any diff must be analyzed and accepted as part of the PR. This catches semantic drift even where no test asserts an error, and burning down the remaining baseline diffs will make the Go compiler 99.999 percent compatible - down to the exact error-message format.

key_points: Port, do not rewrite - only a port reproduces the semantics in excruciating detail.
Parse, bind, and emit are embarrassingly parallel; check runs as independent checkers over an immutable program view.
Deterministic output beats using every core - errors must not change with the machine.
Pool-allocating AST nodes in chunks of 256 cut allocations by two orders of magnitude.
Native code removes JIT sponginess - profiles get deterministic and pprof finds the hotspots.
A type checker's output is error messages, and better checking can break your build.
WASM gives the gains back for now - Go needs stack switching that WASM cannot do yet.
Backwards compatibility is king: every version is as compatible as every other.
Do not spend the 10x on 10x more complex types - you can run Doom in the type checker, but please do not.
